Tisha b'Av. The Ninth of Av is a day of mourning and fasting observed in July or August. It commemorates the destruction of both Jewish Temples—the First Temple by the Babylonians in five hundred eighty-six BCE and the Second Temple by the Romans in seventy CE—as well as other calamities in Jewish history. The day marks the lowest point in the Jewish calendar's cycle of commemoration.

A twenty-five-hour fast parallels Yom Kippur in duration, though Tisha b'Av is observed as a day of mourning rather than atonement. The Book of Lamentations is read during evening services, using a mournful melody that emphasizes the sorrow and loss commemorated by the day. Sitting on the floor or low stools and wearing black or dark clothing are traditional signs of mourning observed during the holiday.

The day is considered inauspicious in Jewish tradition; major calamities, including the Bar Kokhba revolt's final defeat and the expulsion from Spain, are traditionally dated to this day. Unlike other fast days, work and study of Torah except mourning-related texts are prohibited on Tisha b'Av, emphasizing its gravity. The Kaddish prayer is recited in a special form, and kinot, elegies specific to the day, are chanted during services.

The Temple's destruction ended the sacrificial system and transformed Jewish practice toward prayer and study rather than Temple-centered worship. Paradoxically, Jewish tradition teaches that the Messiah will be born on Tisha b'Av, making the day one of potential future redemption despite present sorrow. This focus on the primary destruction of the Temples reflects Jewish memory and resilience through trauma and displacement.
